Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "The family’s photo catalogue began with six shoeboxes on the dining-room table and a question no one could answer: which of the many prints showed the same occasion? Mara had inherited the boxes from her grandmother, Elsie Vale, and wanted a record that would help the family identify people and places without turning the collection into a formal archive. Her brother Peter brought a scanner, while their cousin Jo arrived with a notebook and a tin of adhesive labels. They agreed to work through the photographs together before deciding what should be shared beyond the family.

The boxes held images from three generations, from Elsie’s childhood in 1938 to a reunion at the old orchard in 2004. Some photographs had dates written on the back in blue pencil; others carried only a first name or a brief note such as “Sunday at the lake.” The group used those notes as clues, not as proof. When two relatives remembered an event differently, Mara recorded both accounts in the catalogue and left the date uncertain. She also kept the original spelling of names, even when a later family document used a different version.

1. The first pass through the collection

They began by sorting photographs into broad groups: family gatherings, school pictures, holidays, work, and unidentified scenes. The categories were temporary, and no one was asked to settle a photograph’s place in the family history before scanning it. Peter assigned each image a catalogue number and saved a high-resolution file; Jo wrote the number on a removable slip beside the photograph rather than on its back. Mara entered a short description, any visible date, the names people suggested, and the source of each identification. That distinction mattered when an aunt recognized a young man as her father but could not recall where the picture had been taken.

The initial scan produced 684 files, including 73 duplicate scans made when the same print was handled twice or scanned at more than one size. The working catalogue therefore listed 611 distinct photographs, not 684 separate family images. Mara kept the duplicate files in a review folder until Peter had checked that they were exact copies; a pair that differed in crop or contrast remained available for comparison. The total described the photographs in the boxes, not every image the family had ever owned. Several relatives still had albums at home, and the group had not yet examined them.

Elsie’s handwriting supplied a useful but uneven guide. On one envelope she had written “Ruth, June 1952,” though no one in the family knew a Ruth of that generation. Peter thought the name might refer to Elsie’s neighbor, while Jo remembered hearing that a cousin had visited that summer. They entered “Ruth, possibly a neighbor or cousin” in the identification field and kept the envelope with the related prints. In another case, a note naming “the station” could refer to either the railway platform in Northbridge or the bus depot near the market. The location stayed unresolved rather than being chosen for convenience.

The catalogue also recorded physical details that might help someone locate the original print. A description could note a torn lower corner, a pale mark across the sky, or the faint impression of a studio stamp. The group did not treat those marks as evidence of a date unless there was a sound reason to do so. For example, the photographer’s address on one studio portrait matched a directory entry that placed the business on Willow Street in 1947. That gave them a likely range, but not a confirmed year, so the catalogue described the image as “probably mid-1940s” and linked the directory reference in a notes field.

As they worked, the family established a small set of conventions. Each catalogue entry used one number, even if the same photograph appeared in more than one subject group. Names were entered as the family members supplied them, with alternate spellings noted separately rather than silently substituted. A question mark indicated a tentative identification, while “unknown” meant that no one had offered a plausible name. They used “not dated” only when the print and accompanying material gave no useful clue; where evidence suggested a period, they recorded the range and explained why. These choices made the entries readable without disguising what the family did not know.

Mara’s notes from the second afternoon include a disagreement about a picnic photograph. Her father identified the woman standing beside Elsie as his aunt Beatrice, but Peter thought she looked more like Elsie’s friend Nora. Jo found a letter from 1961 that mentioned both women attending an orchard picnic, but it did not say which one was in the photograph. They entered both suggestions and attached the letter as a related document. Mara later told the group, “I’d rather leave two names in the notes than make one sound certain.” No one objected, and they moved on to the next print.

Before sharing the catalogue, they reviewed what it contained about living relatives. A few descriptions mentioned a family move, a health-related absence, or a private nickname that might be uncomfortable outside the household. The group kept those details in a restricted notes file and used more general wording in the version intended for relatives. The photographs themselves were not altered, and the access decision applied to the accompanying descriptions, not to the original collection. Mara planned to ask each person named in the sensitive entries before adding those notes to a wider family copy.

The catalogue now has a printed index organized by surname, place, and approximate year, alongside a digital spreadsheet with links to the scanned files. Peter stored one copy on an external drive kept at his home and another with Mara; the family has not chosen a public hosting service. Jo added a column for the box and sleeve where each original print can be found, which lets someone return to the physical collection without searching every container. The labels remain on removable slips, and the backs of the photographs are still untouched.

A separate envelope contains four photographs that were found inside a book after the boxes had been catalogued. They show a garden, a school doorway, and two unidentified adults; none has a name or date on the back. Jo has recorded where the envelope was discovered, but the photographs have not yet been scanned or assigned catalogue numbers.
